description.purpose: A secret store with no operation that returns a secret. Not a policy layer over a store -- the route surface of the `vault` cell type simply has no read on it: `put`, `use`, `rotate`, `revoke`, `status`, `unlock`, `lock`, and no `get`. A fully compromised model on the other end of an edge can ask the vault to USE a credential inside a granted scope; it cannot ask to see one, because the question has no name here.
description.use_when: Wherever an agent tree needs a credential it must never be able to read -- typically inside an access hive, as the sibling of the cell that validated the grant. Instantiate it INSIDE the hive that owns it and declare it as a non-port interior cell (`params.ports`), so the generic hive-port boundary refuses any edge from outside the scope.
description.not_in_scope: No network code: the vault signs and stores, it does not speak HTTP -- a connector does that. No grant lookup either: a cell cannot query another cell inside one handle(), so the broker validates the grant and the vault checks WHO is talking (its one ACL) and records the grant id it was handed. And no protection against a process that reads its memory while unlocked -- that is closed by placement (own process, own user), which is a deployment property and changes no edge.
examples: PORTS - in_use: an edge from the broker (the cell named in `params.broker`) carrying a `tool_call` turn with {op:'use', use:'sign', name, payload, grant_id}. out_result: the vault's answer back to the broker, a `tool_result` carrying the SIGNATURE and never the secret. There is deliberately no in-port for anything else: a message from any other sender is refused and audited before the operation is looked at.

FILLING - secrets enter over the user channel and nowhere else: `meclaw --vault /main/access/vault --vault-add telegram_token` reads the value from stdin and writes it straight into the vault's own database. No message, no message log row, no context window. The broker itself cannot put -- otherwise an agent that captured the broker could swap the vault's contents for its own.

UNLOCK - `meclaw --vault-key-source` names a SOURCE, never key material (a key on a command line lands in ps output and in shell history). Default `auto`: under systemd it reads $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/vault_key (use LoadCredentialEncrypted=, TPM2-bound where the machine has one); on a terminal it prompts with echo off.

ATTESTATION - before it accepts the key the vault verifies its own inbound edges against `params.broker` + `params.sealed_neighbors`. The birth topology is exempt from mutation gates by design, so an agent with filesystem access could rewrite the tree and let the NEXT BOOT wire itself into the vault. It can. It just never gets the key: an unexpected neighbour leaves the vault LOCKED, and a locked vault is useless to it.

NO-DELETE - a rotation appends a version, a revocation flips a status, and yesterday's ciphertext stays on disk. That is what makes a revocation auditable rather than a hole. `revoke` needs no passphrase: being locked out must never stop you from disabling a credential that leaked.
